items.title: Meta returns to open weights: Muse Glimmer, its first open-weights release since Llama 4, scores 35 ...
items.content:
Meta returns to open weights: Muse Glimmer, its first open-weights release since Llama 4, scores 35 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. It is a 30B-parameter model, and the first from Meta to be released under Apache 2.0

Muse Glimmer (high) arrives 16 months after Llama 4, scoring 21 points above Llama 4 Maverick (14), Meta's last open weights release. It sits alongside Kimi K2.5 (Reasoning, 36) and just behind Qwen3.6 27B (Reasoning, 38) and Ling 3.0 Flash (38), and creates a two-tier Meta lineup together with the proprietary flagship Muse Spark 1.2 (xhigh, 57)

@AIatMeta shared access with us ahead of public release for benchmarking. Congratulations to @AIatMeta, @finkd, and @alexandr_wang on the release!

Key Takeaways:

➤ Meta's open-weights line is back, under its most permissive license yet. Every prior Meta open release shipped under a Llama License; Muse Glimmer uses Apache 2.0, placing almost no restrictions on commercial use or derivatives

➤ Strong intelligence for its parameter count. At 30B parameters, Muse Glimmer scores 5 points above Gemma 4 31B (Reasoning, 30) at the same size, and effectively matches 1T total parameter Kimi K2.5 (Reasoning, 36) with 33x fewer parameters. Qwen3.6 27B (Reasoning, 38) remains ahead on the Intelligence vs Parameters frontier at a slightly smaller size

➤ Small enough to self-host on a single GPU, even at full context. Muse Glimmer is a 30B dense model (including a ~1.8B vision encoder) with weights at ~60 GB in BF16 and ~18 GB in 4-bit. It features a hybrid-attention mechanism with three sliding-window layers for every global layer, which holds KV cache memory use to ~1.8 GB (minimum) at its pre-extension 128K context. This means the model can run at full context on a single H100 at BF16 precision, or on a higher-spec MacBook or RTX 5090 at 4-bit, with more breathing room if the vision encoder is not required

➤ Agentic knowledge work is its weakness relative to its size class. Muse Glimmer scores 953 Elo on GDPval-AA v2, below the 1,000 human baseline and behind other models at its intelligence level, including the similarly sized Qwen3.6 27B (Reasoning, 1141), and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (1141). Knowledge calibration follows the same pattern: its AA-Omniscience Index of -33 is low for its intelligence level, driven by an 82% hallucination rate (Qwen3.6 27B: 49%) rather than accuracy, where it matches its peers. Agentic tool use is the exception, with Muse Glimmer scoring 24% on Tau3-Banking, ahead of Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (18%) and Qwen3.6 27B (17%), among the best in its class

Other model details:

➤ Parameters: 30B Dense
➤ Context window: 128K tokens, plus extension
➤ License: Apache 2.0
➤ Openness Index: 44, indicating relatively high openness/transparency vs. other major open-weights models
➤ Pricing and output speed: at the time of release, Meta is not serving the model on their API; pricing and serving speed are TBC depending on third-party providers

items.content:
People hate that many of us aren't reading AI code anymore.

To them, if we aren't looking at the code, we must be deploying garbage. Or whatever we are building must be too simple or useless.

A little bit of background:

We are working on a large system, and both Claude Code and Codex are now handling 99% of it.

We started building this around 5 years ago, and it's all deployed on AWS. Some of the services we are using are SageMaker, Lambda functions, DynamoDB, RDS, SQS, CloudWatch, Step Functions, and ECS.

The system supports the continuous training of about a dozen custom vision models that we use to process data sent by customers.

Little by little, agentic coding has been taking over to the point where we aren't checking the code manually anymore.

Agentic coding has gotten to a point where the ratio between time spent reading the code and bugs found is no longer worth it to us.

Instead, we are using that time to design ways to verify the system using a combination of automated code reviews and unit, integration, and acceptance tests.

Are we finding problems in the code generated by the agents? Yes, frequently.

Would we catch those problems by checking the code manually? Maybe, but not without a significant investment of time.

The fact that we don't read the code manually doesn't mean we are deploying garbage: we are verifying everything we push live; we just stopped looking at the lines because the signal-to-noise ratio doesn't make sense anymore.

I believe many people who aren't here yet will move to a similar approach over the next 6, 12, or 18 months. Others will continue typing code by hand, and that's okay.

@glitchtruth @KyleCranmer It was running Widrow's supervised Adaline procedure initially, using a pre-determined pseudo-random bit sequence known by the transmitter and receiver modems.
But then it switched to Bob Lucky's self-supervised Adaline procedure in which the weighted sum was self-supervised by its own binary thresholded version.
This allowed the modem to automatically track slowly-changing characteristics of the line.
Bob Lucky and his collaborators at Bell Labs implemented a mixed analog-digital version of this in which the weighted sums were computed in analog, but the weights were coded on 8 bits, implemented by 8 relays.
It was easy to hear whether the procedure had converged by listening to the number of relay clicks per unit time.
Bob Lucky was the Executive Director of Bell Labs Division 113, in which I was hired in 1988 (in the Adaptive Systems Research Department, BL11315).

items.title: Long-running AI systems often discover halfway through a task that the original plan, constraints, o...
items.content:
Long-running AI systems often discover halfway through a task that the original plan, constraints, or even the working objective were wrong, yet allowing them to change direction freely makes it hard to distinguish sensible correction from simply lowering the bar after failure.

The Argus system presented in this paper is built around that problem: it is a runtime—the software around a fixed AI model that manages its work, memory, tools, and checks—that keeps a durable record across many separate work sessions and divides responsibility among a manager, planner, engineer, and reviewer.

Changes to objectives, reusable procedures, memories, or rejected approaches are kept only when supported by evidence and approved by the role responsible for that decision, so a failed attempt can become useful information without quietly rewriting the task.

The authors test this design across software engineering, GPU optimization, model training, research tasks, mathematical work, paper production, hardware design, and materials research; on SWE-Bench Pro, for example, Argus reports about 78% task completion versus 59% for a direct model-based baseline, while later parts of the run use fewer tokens and less active time than the early parts.

Chinese billionaire Zhang Lei thinks the AI industry is powering its data centers the wrong way.

His company, Envision, just built what it calls the world’s first AI data center running entirely on off-grid wind and solar, tucked into China’s Inner Mongolia region as part of a plan he’s dubbed Mission Gobi.

The bet is that cheap desert renewables, paired with massive batteries, can run servers around the clock without touching a strained power grid.

Zhang has promised 5 GW of these facilities by 2030.

There are still questions around water-free cooling and the cost of battery storage, and Western governments are wary of Chinese infrastructure.

Zhang brushes off Western worries, seeing the same desert model working in dry parts of Spain. 

He also says the tech is “kind of a civilizational output for the rest of the world.”

items.content:
A missile engineer got tired of mosquitoes... so he built an autonomous drone that hunts them

Malaria kills over 600,000 people every year, most of them children under 5, so this could save millions of lives

Here's how it works:

> Each drone weighs 40 grams (lighter than a golf ball)

> It fires ultrasonic pulses and listens through an array of tiny microphones, reading the Doppler signature of an insect's wings

> That signal lets it tell a mosquito apart from a bee, then chase the target down and intercept it mid-air with propellers

The company is backed by YC, and the founder previously engineered guidance and navigation systems for missiles. It's a legitimate project.

They believe 10 drones could clear an entire square kilometre, cutting the cost of mosquito control by 100x

So far though, the only public demo (below) was killing a moth in an enclosed room. Whether it works on a mosquito in the wild is the real test ahead

items.content:
Tiny, specialized, and open models are the future!

The TwiL-LM family of models is now available on HuggingFace for Transformers and llama.cpp, under a non-commercial license.

To give you an idea of how good these tiny models are:

1. The 3B version beats OpenAI's 120B gpt-oss model on 4/5 formal-reasoning benchmarks, despite being 40x smaller.

2. The 3B version is 2.6x faster than gpt-oss-120b in webAI's throughput tests.

3. The 1.7B version is only 1.06 GB and runs locally on phones and laptops at ~367 tokens/sec.

These models are built specifically for deductive reasoning, structured outputs, tool calling, and logic verification, rather than trying to be a general-purpose LLM.

items.content:
comments like this on the aie channel miss the point.

- we are building a community and an industry that is bigger than any one person can hold in their head. your slop is someone's aha moment and vice versa.
- speakers spend quality time coming and presenting their strongest beliefs/entire year's work in 20-180 minutes
- we spend millions on union AV labor and editing to get our speakers a public record that they can then send to customers, employees, and investors
- our speakers are mostly engineers, researchers, academics and founders doing the work; not polished professional talking heads doing the circuit. most talks are prepped <1 week before. most have had ~0 public speaking training. 
- if you want the polished ppl, many other conferences select for people whose main job it is to be great speakers who give great talks
- if you only judge quality by view count, you are guaranteed to be cooked by the algorithm. you will only ever hear about things after they are popular; worse; you consider things good only because they are popular. there are entire industries dedicated to manipulating you. do better.

that said:
- we CAN do a better job in curation. that's on me.
- we CAN do a better job in coaching. also on me.
- we CAN do a better job in production. that's on our team.
- we COULD publish some talks to a secondary channel... I'm just concerned for those speakers as that will start form a smaller base, advice welcome, i am constantly pressured to do this every single year and have said no so far

RLHF is a powerful approach to AI alignment and human-centered machine learning. By combining reinforcement learning algorithms with human feedback signals, RLHF has become a key method for improving the safety, reliability, and alignment of large language models (LLMs).

To be fair they're not the prettiest (ro...
items.content:
Got 3x Xiaomi Smart Air Purifier Elite, one for each floor

To be fair they're not the prettiest (round and silver) but they're about the most powerful ones you can get, being able to clean 600 m³/hour for spaces up to 125 m², so essentially one big floor

The best part though is the bigger the air purifier, the more silent they are, you just simply don't hear them, they're on Auto mode and unless the air gets really bad they won't spin up (so in my case they never spin up)

Then I got a small one for the bedroom, the Xiaomi Smart Air Purifier 4, this one's actually just square and white and pretty

Anyway here's the data before and after installing them, AQI went down from 59 in the gym, or about smoking 1 cigarette per day, to 22 (clean air)

P.S. I bought Xiaomi based on the QT thread below, it's great, they actually have their own Home Assistant repo on GitHub which is how every smart home device should be: open and limitless! No bs API limits with 🇨🇳 Xiaomi unlike with 🇯🇵 Daikin (max 150 reqs/day) which tells you all you need to know about the modernity of Chinese tech vs the absolute stoneage levels of Japanese tech!

inb4 "omg Chinese devices phone home" no you can just run these locally on your Home Assistant!

Which is wild cause we live near the ocean in Portugal far from any city and you still have to deal with somewhat dirty air, it's just the reality of modern life. Now imagine what you breath in living in the city?

My aunt died of lung cancer at 55, you never know why but she did live in a big Dutch port city with lots of container ships all day every day exhausting dirty oil fumes, so clean air is a priority for me (another reason I couldn't keep living in Bali and Thailand)

One thing that's still bad is VOC levels (volatile organic compounds), today I learnt you can only get rid of that with carbon filters, no regular HEPA air purifier will help you with that (just like it won't help you with CO2, you just have to open the window or build a fresh air inlet into your house)

Anyway, cleaner air, hooray! 💨

I was a Soviet Union collapse kid, so I grew up on video-salons of the 1990s and Hollywood movies.

I learned one thing from these movies: never speak to the police without your lawyer present, and the only thing you should say if the police are trying to talk to you is, "I need my lawyer." I'm always teaching my kids to behave this way, though we are in Canada.

Since my childhood, I have been certain of two facts: 1) All Americans have a lawyer, and 2) each American has a black suit/dress and a black umbrella for funerals.

After watching Netflix true crime documentaries, I realized that 99% of Americans talk to the police without a lawyer, making dozens of mistakes and incriminating themselves, voluntarily take the polygraph, then get accused of crimes they incriminated themselves with by their own talking, and only then call the lawyer.

My world is half broken.

I hope they still have a black suit and a black umbrella for funerals!
